_about: Simple-language Explain Like I am 10 overrides (scripts/build-batch-b.py).
Klamath_River_Dam_Removal.html: Dams are walls across rivers. On the Klamath River, four big dams stopped salmon from swimming upstream for about 100 years.
In 2024 all four dams were taken out.
Now salmon can swim to more than 400 miles of river again, and people are planting new plants where the old lakes were.
Elwha_River_Restoration.html: The Elwha River had two dams that stopped salmon from swimming home.
Between 2011 and 2014 both dams were taken down.
Sand and gravel stuck behind the dams washed down the river and helped rebuild the beach, and the river runs free again.
Living_Lands_and_Waters.html: Living Lands & Waters is a team that lives on a big boat called a barge.
They travel down rivers and pick up trash with help from volunteers.
They have picked up more than 14 million pounds of trash and planted millions of trees.
American_Rivers.html: American Rivers is a group that helps take out old dams that are not needed anymore.
When a dam comes out, fish can swim up the river again.
In 2025, 100 dams came out in the U.S., freeing almost 5,000 miles of river.
Lake_Erie_Algal_Bloom_Forecast.html: Sometimes tiny green living things called algae grow so much in Lake Erie that the water turns green.
Some of this algae makes poison that can get into drinking water.
NOAA watches the lake from space and from boats and warns people where the bad water is, like a weather report.
Alliance_for_the_Great_Lakes_Adopt_a_Bea: Adopt-a-Beach is when people go to a beach on the Great Lakes and pick up trash.
Most of the trash they find is plastic.
They also write down what they find, so scientists can learn where the trash comes from.
Global_Forest_Watch.html: Global Forest Watch is a free map of the world's forests made from satellite pictures.
When trees are cut down, the map sends an alert.
People who live in forests use the alerts to stop illegal cutting fast.
Rainforest_Connection.html: Rainforest Connection puts listening boxes high up in trees.
The boxes use the sun for power and a computer that can tell when it hears a chainsaw.
When it hears one, a ranger gets a message on a phone and can go stop the cutting.
One_Tree_Planted.html: One Tree Planted is a group that plants trees all over the world.
They work with local helpers and check on the trees for three years to make sure they grow.
They have planted more than 171 million trees in 84 countries.
Global_Fishing_Watch.html: Big fishing ships sail all over the ocean, and many of them are hard to see.
Global Fishing Watch uses pictures from space and smart computers to find them.
They put the map online for free, so everyone can see where fishing happens and protect the ocean.
TEMPO.html: TEMPO is a space tool that checks how dirty the air is.
It stays above the same spot on Earth and looks at North America every hour while the sun is up.
This helps warn people on bad air days so they can stay safe.
Zero_Debris_Charter.html: Space junk is old satellites and broken pieces still flying around Earth.
The Zero Debris Charter is a promise to stop making new space junk by 2030.
Many space companies and countries signed it so useful satellites can stay safe.
BepiColombo.html: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
BepiColombo is really two spacecraft that rode there together for eight years.
In 2026 they start circling Mercury to learn what it is made of.
Hayabusa2_Torifune.html: Hayabusa2 is a Japanese spacecraft that once brought pieces of an asteroid back to Earth.
In July 2026 it zoomed past another asteroid, Torifune, closer than any spacecraft ever flew past a space rock.
Aiming that well means we could one day hit a dangerous asteroid and push it away.
Psyche.html: Psyche is a NASA spacecraft flying to an asteroid that might be made of a lot of metal.
In 2026 it swung past Mars to get a speed boost.
It gets there in 2029 and will help us learn what the center of a planet is like.
Lucy.html: Lucy is a NASA spacecraft that visits many asteroids, one after another.
Some asteroids travel with Jupiter around the Sun. They are very old.
Studying them is like reading fossils of how the planets were made.
Comet_Interceptor.html: Some comets come from very far away and have never been near the Sun before.
Comet Interceptor will wait in space until scientists find one.
Then three spacecraft fly past it together to make a 3D picture.
EnVision.html: Venus is about the same size as Earth, but it is hot enough to melt lead.
EnVision is a spacecraft that will study Venus from deep inside to the top of its air.
It may tell us how a planet like ours got so hot.
SPHEREx.html: SPHEREx is a space telescope that takes pictures of the whole sky.
It sees 102 colors of light that our eyes cannot see.
Those colors show where frozen water hides in space.
Sentinel-4.html: Sentinel-4 is a space tool that watches the air over Europe.
It stays above the same spot and checks the air every hour.
This helps warn people when the air is dirty.
SARSAT.html: Boats, planes and hikers can carry a small emergency beacon.
If they are in trouble, the beacon sends a signal that satellites hear.
The satellites tell rescuers where to go, and that has saved thousands of people.
Coral_IVF.html: Once a year, corals let out tiny eggs into the sea at the same time.
Scientists catch them and help millions of baby corals grow in special pools.
Then they put the babies on hurt reefs so the reefs can grow back.
Posidonia_Meadows.html: Posidonia is a sea grass that grows under the Mediterranean Sea.
Some patches have been growing for more than 2,000 years.
They hold carbon in the sand and give baby fish a safe home.
Whales_Ocean_Gardeners.html: Whales eat deep in the ocean and then poop near the top.
Their poop is like plant food for tiny ocean plants.
Those plants feed fish and help take carbon out of the air.
Justdiggit.html: In some dry places, rain runs off the hard ground instead of soaking in.
Justdiggit helps people dig little smile-shaped holes that catch the rain.
Then grass and trees grow back and the land turns green.
River_Cleanup.html: River Cleanup is a group that picks up trash in rivers.
More than a million helpers have joined.
Catching trash in rivers stops it from reaching the ocean.
Great_Green_Wall.html: The Sahara desert is next to a dry area called the Sahel.
Many African countries are planting and protecting trees and grass there.
They want to make a long green belt across Africa.
Veggie_Space_Garden.html: Astronauts live on the space station for months.
Veggie is a little garden with special lights that grows lettuce in space.
In 2015 astronauts ate a salad they grew there.
Tsunami_Early_Warning.html: A tsunami is a group of giant waves, usually made when a big earthquake shakes the sea floor.
Buoys, satellites and special computers watch the ocean and tell warning centers when a tsunami is coming.
If the ground shakes hard or the sea pulls back fast near a beach, go to high ground right away.
Coral_Gardeners.html: Coral reefs are like busy underwater cities for fish, and many are getting sick from hot water.
Coral Gardeners grow baby corals in underwater nurseries, like a garden.
When the corals are big enough, divers plant them back on the reef so it can grow again.
Project_Seagrass.html: Seagrass is a real plant with flowers that grows underwater near the coast.
Its meadows give baby fish a safe home and keep the water clean.
Project Seagrass plants seagrass seeds to grow the meadows back.
FreshWater_Watch.html: Rivers and lakes can get dirty in ways you cannot see.
FreshWater Watch gives people simple test kits to check the water.
Scientists and governments use the results to find problems and fix them.
Rewilding_Europe.html: Rewilding means letting nature take care of itself again.
Rewilding Europe helps bring back big animals like bison, which keep forests and meadows healthy.
People can visit these wild places, which helps the villages nearby.
Globe_at_Night.html: At night, city lights can hide the stars.
Globe at Night asks people to go outside, find a group of stars and say how many they can see.
All those answers show where the sky is too bright, so we can fix it.
CO2M.html: Some gases, like carbon dioxide, trap heat and warm our planet.
CO2M will be three satellites that measure how much of these gases people release.
That helps countries see if their plans to cut pollution are working.
Mission_Blue_Hope_Spots.html: A Hope Spot is a special place in the ocean that needs protecting.
People who live nearby pick it and help take care of it.
There are now 168 Hope Spots in 115 countries.
FireSat.html: Wildfires are much easier to stop while they are still small.
FireSat satellites carry special cameras that can sense heat from space.
They can spot a fire about the size of two parking spaces and help firefighters act fast.
Eden_People_Planet.html: Eden helps people bring back forests and wild land near their homes.
In Tanzania, people from 40 villages are helping protect a huge mountain area.
Healthy forests keep water clean and give animals a place to live.
Waterkeeper_Alliance.html: A Waterkeeper is a person or group who watches over a river, lake or coast.
They check the water and stop people from polluting it.
It all started with fishermen who saved the Hudson River in New York.
SeaTrees.html: "Seatrees" are ocean plants like mangroves, kelp and seagrass.
SeaTrees helps people plant and protect them with help from local teams.
These plants give fish a home and protect beaches from big storms.
Living_Lakes.html: Living Lakes is a team of groups that look after lakes all over the world.
They clean up trash and help people near lakes earn money without harming nature.
In Mongolia they help protect a lake that is about 2 million years old.
EMIT.html: EMIT is a special camera on the International Space Station.
It splits sunlight into many colors to tell what the ground is made of.
It also spotted big leaks of methane, a gas that heats the planet, so they can be fixed.
GEDI.html: GEDI is a laser tool on the International Space Station.
It shines light down on forests and times how long it takes to bounce back.
That tells scientists how tall trees are and how much carbon forests hold.
OCO-2.html: OCO-2 is a satellite that measures carbon dioxide in the air.
It shows where the gas comes from and where plants and oceans soak it up.
It can even see plants glow faintly, which shows how healthy they are.
Sentinel-5P.html: Sentinel-5P is a satellite that sniffs the air from space.
Every day it checks the whole planet for gases that make air dirty.
This helps keep people healthy and track gases that warm Earth.
PREFIRE.html: PREFIRE is two tiny satellites about the size of a shoebox.
They measure heat leaving the Arctic and Antarctica that our eyes can't see.
That helps scientists understand melting ice and make better weather forecasts.
HydroGNSS.html: Navigation satellites send signals that bounce off the ground.
HydroGNSS catches those echoes to tell how wet the soil is.
That helps farmers, flood planners and scientists watch Earth's water.
Sentinel-3.html: Sentinel-3 satellites check the oceans, land and ice all the time.
They measure how warm the sea is, how high it is, and even spot fires.
Weather and ocean forecasters use this to keep people safe.
Libera.html: Sunlight brings energy to Earth, and Earth sends some back to space.
Libera will measure how much energy leaves our planet each day.
If more comes in than goes out, Earth warms, so this helps track climate.
Surfrider_Foundation.html: Surfrider is a group of people who love the beach and want it clean.
Volunteers pick up trash so it doesn't hurt sea animals.
They also count what they find to help stop plastic at the source.
Heal_the_Bay.html: Heal the Bay helps keep the beaches and ocean near Los Angeles clean.
Thousands of volunteers pick up trash on special cleanup days.
They also run a small aquarium where kids meet local sea animals.
Plastic_Odyssey.html: In many places there is nowhere to recycle plastic, so it ends up in the sea.
Plastic Odyssey helps people build small recycling factories.
They turn old plastic into useful things, like paving stones, and create jobs.
Trout_Unlimited.html: Trout and salmon need cold, clean rivers to live.
Trout Unlimited fixes damaged streams and removes things that block fish.
More than 20,000 volunteers help care for rivers.
Chesapeake_Bay_Foundation.html: The Chesapeake Bay is a huge bay fed by many rivers.
Oysters clean the water, so this group grows and plants millions of them.
They also plant trees by streams and teach students outdoors.
Keep_Tahoe_Blue.html: Lake Tahoe is famous for its clear blue water.
After the Fourth of July, volunteers clean up beaches so trash doesn't reach the lake.
Keep Tahoe Blue uses science to keep the lake clear for people and fish.
American_Forests.html: American Forests is one of the oldest forest groups in the United States.
It plants trees in big forests and in city neighborhoods that need shade.
Trees clean the air, cool hot streets and give animals homes.
Plant-for-the-Planet.html: A 9-year-old boy named Felix asked kids to plant a million trees in every country.
Now more than 100,000 young people have learned to help forests and climate.
The group has planted over 12 million trees in Mexico's Mayan forests.
Dragonfly.html: Dragonfly is like a giant drone with eight rotors.
It will fly to Titan, a moon of Saturn with a thick, hazy sky.
It will look for the kinds of chemistry that came before life on Earth.
International_Charter.html: When a big flood or earthquake happens, rescuers need a map fast.
Space agencies around the world agree to point their satellites at the disaster.
They give the pictures away for free, so helpers know where people need them.
Copernicus_EMS.html: When a disaster happens, helpers need to know which roads and houses are damaged.
Copernicus EMS uses satellite pictures to draw those maps quickly.
It works day and night and has helped more than 120 countries.
FIRMS.html: Satellites can feel the heat of a fire from space.
FIRMS puts those hot spots on a free map within a few hours.
Firefighters and farmers can even get an email when a fire starts nearby.
UNEP_MARS.html: Methane is a gas that heats the planet, and big leaks can be seen from space.
The United Nations watches satellite data and tells countries and companies about leaks.
When they fix a leak, the air gets cleaner and the planet heats up less.
GLOBE_Program.html: GLOBE lets kids and grown-ups do real science outside.
You look at clouds, trees or soil and send what you see with an app.
Scientists use your measurements to understand our planet.
Argo.html: Argo floats are robots that sink deep into the ocean and come back up.
On the way they measure how warm and how salty the water is.
They send the numbers to a satellite, and anyone can use them for free.
Argos.html: Scientists put a tiny radio tag on a turtle, bird or whale.
Satellites pick up the tag's signal and work out where the animal is.
Knowing where animals travel helps people protect them.
Coral_Reef_Watch.html: Corals are tiny animals that build reefs, and too much heat makes them turn white.
NOAA satellites check the ocean's temperature every day.
Reef managers use the warnings to protect corals before it is too late.
RCM.html: RCM is three satellites that use radar, like a bat uses sound.
Radar works in the dark and sees through clouds and smoke.
It helps ships find safe paths through ice and helps after floods.
ATLAS.html: ATLAS is four robot telescopes that scan the night sky.
They look for space rocks that come close to Earth.
An early warning gives people time to get ready or move away.
Pan-STARRS.html: Pan-STARRS is two big telescopes on a mountain in Maui.
Their giant cameras photograph the sky to find moving space rocks.
Finding them early keeps Earth safe.
Catalina_Sky_Survey.html: Catalina is a team in Arizona that hunts for space rocks every clear night.
They have found more near-Earth asteroids than anyone else.
They even spotted a small one hours before it burned up over Africa.
ESA_NEOCC.html: Some asteroids pass near Earth, and scientists need to know where they will go.
ESA's centre in Italy collects telescope data and works out their paths.
If an asteroid ever looks dangerous, they warn emergency teams.
EFFIS.html: EFFIS warns when the weather makes forest fires likely.
After a fire, satellites show exactly how much land burned.
Countries use this to fight fires and plan how forests recover.
JPSS.html: JPSS satellites fly over the North and South Poles, around and around.
They scan the whole Earth twice a day for temperature, clouds and rain.
Forecasters use the data to warn people before hurricanes and blizzards.
GSMaP.html: GSMaP is a map that shows where it is raining all over the world.
It mixes data from many satellites and updates every hour.
Scientists use it to watch rain as it falls and to study climate.
CAMS.html: CAMS checks the air all over the world, from smoke to dust to pollution.
It uses satellites and computer models to forecast dirty air days ahead.
People can plan to stay safe on bad air days.
GloFAS.html: GloFAS predicts when rivers might flood, up to a month ahead.
It uses weather forecasts and computer models of rivers.
Early warnings give families time to move to safety.
Copernicus_Marine.html: Copernicus Marine is like a weather service for the ocean.
It shows ocean temperature, currents, sea ice and tiny plant life.
Sailors, scientists and fishers use it for free.
OpenET.html: Plants drink water and breathe it out into the air.
OpenET uses satellites to measure how much water every field uses.
Farmers can then water only what crops need and save water.
Parker_Solar_Probe.html: Parker Solar Probe is a spacecraft that flies closer to the Sun than any other.
A thick heat shield keeps it safe from the Sun's heat.
It helps scientists learn about solar storms that can affect satellites on Earth.
SOHO.html: SOHO is a spacecraft that has watched the Sun every day for 30 years.
It sits in a special spot in space where it can always see the Sun.
Its pictures help people get ready for solar storms.
CryoSat.html: CryoSat is a satellite that measures how thick the ice is near the North and South Poles.
It uses radar to spot tiny changes in the height of the ice.
Knowing how ice changes helps scientists understand sea level rise.
International_Coastal_Cleanup.html: Every year, people around the world clean trash off beaches and rivers on the same day.
They also write down what they find.
That list helps find ways to stop trash from reaching the ocean.
The_SeaCleaners.html: The SeaCleaners use special boats called Mobulas to scoop plastic out of the water.
They work with local people so the cleanup keeps going after they leave.
Some of the plastic is recycled into useful things, like walkways.
WeForest.html: WeForest helps whole areas of land grow back into healthy forests.
It works with local families so trees and people can both thrive.
It has grown more than 118 million trees so far.
Meteosat_Third_Generation.html: Meteosat Third Generation is a team of weather satellites that watch Europe and Africa.
One camera takes a new picture of the weather every 2.5 minutes.
Another camera spots lightning, which helps warn people about dangerous storms.
SMAP.html: SMAP is a satellite that measures how wet or dry the ground is.
It can also tell if the soil is frozen or thawed.
This helps farmers and scientists get ready for floods and droughts.
GCOM-C.html: GCOM-C, also called SHIKISAI, is a Japanese satellite that looks at the whole Earth.
It sees clouds, tiny particles in the air, plants, ocean color, snow and ice.
This helps scientists understand climate change.
London_Tideway_Tunnel.html: When it rains hard in London, old sewers used to overflow into the River Thames.
A giant new tunnel under the river now catches that dirty water.
The water is sent away to be cleaned, so the river stays healthier.
Penobscot_River_Restoration.html: Dams on the Penobscot River blocked fish from swimming up to lay their eggs.
People took out two dams and built new ways for fish to get past others.
Now millions of fish swim up the river again each year.
Kissimmee_River_Restoration.html: Long ago, people dug a straight canal through the curvy Kissimmee River.
That stopped floods but hurt the wetlands, birds and fish.
Now workers have filled parts of the canal so the river can curve and flood its wetlands again.
Voyager.html: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are two spacecraft that left Earth in 1977.
They flew past the giant planets and are now outside the bubble the Sun makes around itself.
On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 will be so far away that its radio signal takes a whole day to reach us.
FORUM.html: Earth gives off heat into space as invisible infrared light.
Part of that light, called far-infrared, has never been measured from space.
FORUM will measure it, helping scientists understand how Earth keeps its heat balance.
CIMR.html: CIMR will be two satellites that measure the ocean and polar sea ice.
They use a huge round antenna to sense tiny amounts of natural microwave energy.
They will cover almost the whole Earth every day, even through clouds.
CRISTAL.html: CRISTAL is a satellite that will measure how thick the polar sea ice is.
It will also measure how deep the snow is on top of the ice.
It carries on the work of the CryoSat satellite.
CHIME.html: CHIME will be two satellites that see far more colours than our eyes can.
Those colours show how healthy crops and soils are.
Farmers and scientists can use this to grow food and protect nature.
GeoXO.html: GeoXO will be new weather satellites that stay over the same spot above Earth.
They will watch storms, wildfires, smoke and floods as they happen.
This helps forecasters warn people sooner.
INSAT-3DS.html: INSAT-3DS is an Indian weather satellite that stays over the same place above Earth.
It takes pictures of clouds, rain, fog and fires.
It also passes on distress calls so rescuers can find people in trouble.
Galileo.html: Galileo is a group of satellites that tells your phone exactly where it is.
Each satellite has very accurate atomic clocks.
Galileo satellites can also hear emergency beacons and pass the alert to rescuers.
Ariel.html: Ariel is a space telescope that will look at planets around other stars.
When a planet passes in front of its star, starlight shines through its air.
Ariel reads that light to find out what the planet's air is made of.
Forest_Elephants.html: Forest elephants live in the rainforests of central and West Africa.
As they walk and eat, they push over and munch small trees.
That leaves room for big, heavy trees that store more carbon.
Yellowstone_Wolves.html: Wolves disappeared from Yellowstone National Park for almost 70 years.
Scientists now study how wolves, elk and other animals live together again.
Coral_Vita.html: Coral reefs are dying in many places around the world.
Coral Vita grows baby corals in tanks on land, where they grow very fast.
Then divers plant them back on damaged reefs.
Arbor_Day_Foundation.html: The Arbor Day Foundation is a group that plants trees.
It has helped plant more than 500 million trees.
Trees clean the air, give animals homes and help cool the planet.
Namami_Gange.html: The Ganga is a huge, holy river in India.
Too much dirty water from towns was flowing into it.
India is building treatment plants to clean that water before it reaches the river.
Clean_Lakes_Alliance.html: Madison, Wisconsin, has five lakes connected by the Yahara River.
Too much phosphorus washes in and feeds smelly algae blooms.
Volunteers check the lakes and the group helps pay for projects to keep them clean.
Sea_Turtle_Conservancy.html: Sea turtles are ancient animals that swim across whole oceans.
Sea Turtle Conservancy protects the beaches where they lay their eggs.
It also tracks turtles with satellites to learn where they go.
Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault.html: Farmers and scientists keep seeds of thousands of crops in places called genebanks.
The Seed Vault on Svalbard keeps a spare copy of those seeds deep inside a frozen mountain.
If a genebank loses its seeds to war or disaster, it can take its copies back and grow them again.
Thwaites_Glacier_Collaboration.html: Thwaites is a giant glacier in Antarctica, the widest on Earth.
It is melting and sliding into the sea, which makes the oceans rise a little.
Scientists went there to find out how fast it could change, so coastal towns can plan.
Carbfix.html: Carbon dioxide is a gas that warms the planet.
Carbfix mixes it with water, like fizzy water, and pumps it deep into volcanic rock.
There the gas reacts with the rock and becomes solid stone that stays put.
African_Parks.html: Some of Africa's national parks were losing their animals because there was not enough money or care.
African Parks works with each country's government to run those parks well.
It brings back animals that had disappeared and helps the people who live nearby.
Digital_Earth_Africa.html: Satellites take pictures of Africa all the time, but the raw data is hard to use.
Digital Earth Africa cleans it up and turns it into ready-made maps.
Anyone can use them for free to track water, crops and coastlines.
Hope_Mars_Mission.html: Hope is a spacecraft from the United Arab Emirates that circles Mars.
It studies the air and weather on Mars, all around the planet.
Scientists everywhere can download its data for free to learn how planets change.
Abu_Dhabi_Mangroves.html: Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water along the coast.
Abu Dhabi is planting millions of them to bring its coastal forests back.
A new website uses satellites and field checks to see how many really grow.
Gaganyaan.html: India wants to send its own astronauts into space.
First, it will fly the crew capsule with a robot called Vyommitra instead of people.
If the test goes well, astronauts can fly on later missions.
NEWater.html: Singapore is a small island without much room to store rain.
So it takes water that has already been used, cleans it with special filters and ultraviolet light, and makes it ultra-clean.
Factories use most of it, and in dry spells some is added to reservoirs.
Cheonggyecheon.html: A stream in the middle of Seoul was covered with concrete and a highway was built on top.
The city took the highway down and opened the stream up again.
Now people walk beside the water in the heart of the city.
Palau_National_Marine_Sanctuary.html: Palau is a country made of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
It decided that most of its ocean should be a place where nobody fishes.
That gives sea life room to grow back and spill over into the areas where local people fish.
Papahanaumokuakea.html: Far out in the ocean past the main Hawaiian islands is a long chain of tiny islands and reefs.
The United States protects the ocean all around them.
Millions of seabirds nest there, and it is a sacred place for Native Hawaiians.
Predator_Free_2050.html: New Zealand's birds grew up with no mammals that hunt them.
Then people brought rats, stoats, possums and cats, which eat birds and their eggs.
The country is working to remove those predators everywhere by 2050.
Galapagos_Giant_Tortoises.html: Giant tortoises once covered the Galápagos Islands, but people and animals they brought nearly wiped them out.
Park rangers and scientists raise baby tortoises in safe centres until they are big enough to survive.
Then they carry them back to the islands where they belong.
MAAP.html: The Amazon rainforest is huge, and it is hard to see where trees are being cut.
Satellites take pictures from space, and MAAP experts compare them to find new clearings.
Then they publish simple reports so governments and everyone else can act.
Mesoamerican_Reef_Insurance.html: Hurricanes can smash coral reefs, and repairs only work if they start quickly.
This insurance pays out automatically when winds reach a set speed, with no long wait.
Trained local teams then use the money to fix the reef.
Costa_Rica_Forest_Payments.html: Forests clean the air, keep water safe and give animals a home.
In Costa Rica the government pays forest owners for those services.
So keeping trees standing becomes worth it for the people who own the land.
Gulf_of_Alaska_Keeper.html: Ocean currents carry nets, ropes and plastic to faraway Alaska beaches where nobody lives.
Gulf of Alaska Keeper crews and volunteers pick it up and pack it into giant bags.
Helicopters lift the bags to a barge, and the trash goes to Anchorage to be recycled or thrown away safely.
Alaska_Kelp_Farming.html: Kelp is a big seaweed that grows fast in cold ocean water.
Alaska farmers grow it on lines in the sea and harvest it each spring and early summer.
It becomes food, farm and beauty products, and it takes up carbon and extra nutrients from the water.
Bristol_Bay_Salmon.html: Bristol Bay in Alaska has rivers full of wild salmon.
A large copper and gold mine was proposed near streams where many of those salmon start life.
The U.S. government limited where mine waste could go, and a judge is now deciding whether that decision stands.
Alaska_SeaLife_Center.html: Sometimes baby seals and sea otters lose their mothers or get hurt.
The Alaska SeaLife Center brings them to Seward and cares for them day and night.
Its scientists also study sea lions and seabirds to learn how the ocean is changing.
South_Georgia_Habitat_Restoration.html: Long ago, ships brought rats and mice to South Georgia, an island near Antarctica.
The rats ate the eggs and chicks of birds that nest on the ground.
A team spread bait across the whole island, and in 2018 it was declared free of rats and mice.
Arctic_Weather_Satellite.html: Weather forecasts need measurements of the air: how warm, how wet, how cloudy.
The Arctic has few weather stations, so satellites do much of the measuring there.
A small test satellite worked so well that Europe is building a whole fleet of them.
GCOM-W_SHIZUKU.html: Sea ice is frozen ocean water that floats around the North and South Poles.
SHIZUKU is a Japanese satellite with a big spinning antenna that "hears" faint microwaves from Earth.
Those signals show where the ice is, even through clouds and in the dark polar winter.
SCISAT.html: High in the sky, a layer of ozone gas blocks most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.
Some human-made chemicals were eating holes in that layer.
SCISAT watches sunlight shine through the air at sunrise and sunset to find out which gases are there.
Chilika_Lake.html: Chilika is a huge lagoon in India where river water and seawater mix.
Mud was choking its link to the sea, so fish and the people who catch them were struggling.
Engineers dug a new opening to the sea, and the fish came back.
Tonle_Sap.html: Tonle Sap is a giant lake in Cambodia joined to the Mekong River.
In the rainy season the river gets so full that water flows backwards into the lake.
The lake swells up, flooding forests where fish grow, and many families live in floating villages.
Lake_Biwa_Soap_Movement.html: Lake Biwa is the biggest lake in Japan.
Phosphorus from washing detergent fed tiny algae until the water turned red in 1977.
People switched to natural soap, and new rules cut the phosphorus going into the lake.
Lake_Constance.html: Lake Constance sits between Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
Too much phosphorus from wastewater made algae grow, which is bad for the lake.
The countries built treatment plants that take out phosphorus, and the lake recovered.
Room_for_the_River.html: When rivers get very full, they can flood towns.
The Netherlands moved dikes back and dug extra channels so the water has more room.
Now high water can spread out safely, and the riverside landscape is better too.
Tubbataha_Reefs.html: Tubbataha is a group of coral reefs far out in the sea in the Philippines.
Nobody is allowed to fish there, so the fish can grow big and have lots of babies.
Baby fish drift out from the reef and help fill fishing grounds around it.
Sargassum_Watch.html: Sargassum is a brown seaweed that floats in big mats on the ocean.
Some years so much of it washes onto beaches that it piles up on the shore.
Scientists use satellites to see where it is, so coastal towns can get ready.
Redonda_Restoration.html: Redonda is a small island in the Caribbean Sea.
Goats and rats had eaten almost everything, so it was bare rock.
People removed them, and plants and birds came back fast.
Iberian_Lynx.html: The Iberian lynx is a wild cat that lives only in Spain and Portugal.
By 2002 there were fewer than 100 left.
Breeding, releases and protection helped, and now there are more than 2,600.
Trees_for_Life.html: The Caledonian forest of pine trees once covered much of the Scottish Highlands.
Today only small pieces are left.
Volunteers plant trees and protect young ones, so the wild forest can grow back.
Nepal_Tigers.html: Tigers were disappearing from Asia because of hunting and lost forests.
Nepal promised to double its tigers, and protected forests and paths between them.
Local communities helped stop poachers, and now Nepal has about three times as many tigers.
Altyn_Dala_Saiga.html: The saiga is an antelope with a big, bendy nose that lives on the grassy steppe.
Not long ago, there were very few left in Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan and its partners protected the steppe, and now there are millions again.
Gorongosa.html: Gorongosa is a big wildlife park in Mozambique, in Africa.
Rangers, scientists and local people work together to protect it.
The latest count found more big animals there than ever recorded.
NEOSSat.html: Some space rocks, called asteroids, pass close to Earth.
NEOSSat is a small Canadian telescope in space that looks for them, even near the Sun.
It also watches satellites and space junk to help avoid crashes in orbit.
Chandrayaan-5_LUPEX.html: Scientists think there may be frozen water hiding near the Moon's south pole.
Japan and India are building a rover to drive there and check.
Knowing where the water is will help plan future human trips to the Moon.
Ross_Sea_MPA.html: The Ross Sea is a cold, wild sea next to Antarctica.
Penguins, seals and whales feed there, and its food chain is still complete.
Countries agreed to make most of it a place where commercial fishing is not allowed.
PROMICE_GC-Net.html: Greenland is covered by a giant sheet of ice.
When it melts or drops icebergs, the sea rises a little.
Weather stations on the ice measure melting and snowfall, so scientists know what is changing.
Iceland_Land_Restoration.html: Long ago, Iceland had more trees and soil.
Cutting wood, sheep grazing, volcanoes and wind blew much of the soil away.
Farmers and the government plant grass, birch and wetlands to hold the soil again.
Emirates_Mission_Asteroid_Belt.html: Between Mars and Jupiter is a belt of space rocks called asteroids.
They are left over from when the planets formed.
A UAE spacecraft will visit seven of them and land on the last one.
Arabian_Oryx.html: The Arabian oryx is a white desert antelope with long, straight horns.
Hunters shot the last wild one in 1972.
Zoos bred them and set them free again, and now about 1,000 live in the wild.
Azraq_Wetland.html: Azraq is an oasis, a wet place in the middle of a desert in Jordan.
People pumped out so much water that it almost dried up.
Conservationists brought water back to pools and returned a tiny fish found nowhere else.
Okavango_Delta.html: The Okavango River flows into Botswana but never reaches the ocean.
Every year its water spreads out across the desert, right in the dry season.
Elephants, lions and birds gather to drink and feed in the new wetland.
Mountain_Gorillas.html: Mountain gorillas live in misty forests on volcanoes in Africa.
Hunting traps and diseases had made them very rare.
Rangers removed traps and vets cared for them, and now there are more.
Seychelles_Marine_Spatial_Plan.html: Seychelles is a country made of islands in the Indian Ocean.
It made a deal: part of its debt was refinanced to pay for ocean protection.
Now almost a third of its sea is protected, bigger than Germany.
Kakapo_Recovery.html: The kākāpō is a big, green parrot from New Zealand that cannot fly.
Rangers watched over every nest and helped chicks grow up, and now there are 325.
Route_of_Parks_Patagonia.html: Patagonia is a wild land of mountains, forests and grass at the bottom of South America.
A conservation group bought land and gave it to Chile.
Chile added even more, and together they made new national parks for everyone.
Danuri_ShadowCam.html: Some craters near the Moon's poles are always dark.
Scientists think frozen water may be hiding inside them.
A super-sensitive camera on a Korean spacecraft takes pictures inside those dark craters.
Cool_Earth_Basic_Income.html: Some families in the Amazon rainforest have very little money.
A charity gave each person a small amount of money every few months, to spend however they wanted.
Families ate better, stayed home instead of leaving for work, and planted and protected more forest.
Andfjorden_MPA.html: Andfjorden is a big, cold stretch of sea in the far north of Norway.
Under the water there are coral reefs, kelp forests and lots of fish, whales and seabirds.
Norway made it a protected area, with extra-strict rules in the most fragile spots.
Atoll_Rewilding.html: Atolls are rings of tiny, low islands made by coral.
Seabirds catch fish at sea and leave droppings full of nutrients on the islands, which wash onto the reef.
Where rats are gone, birds come back, reefs grow faster and the islands get more sand to stay above the waves.
